justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the 1-day estimate of 396, I was anchoring closely to what would have been the prevailing market level at the time of the forecast, assuming no major overnight catalysts and typical mean-reversion tendencies in the short run. The 1-week estimate of 400 reflects a slight upward bias consistent with the longer-run drift in equity markets, while the 1-month estimate of 410 extends that logic further, incorporating a modest risk premium for holding over a longer horizon where compounding and trend continuation become more relevant factors.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. For the 1-day interval, the relatively tight range of 378–414 reflects the fact that intraday and overnight moves in broad equity indices are historically constrained under normal market conditions, with daily moves beyond 2–3% being relatively rare outside of shock events. By the 1-week horizon, the interval widens to account for the possibility of a meaningful macro data release, central bank communication, or geopolitical development shifting sentiment. At 1 month, the interval of 320–500 is quite wide deliberately, as a month is long enough to encompass a full earnings cycle, a Federal Reserve meeting, and numerous unpredictable global developments.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside even my stated intervals include a sudden financial contagion event — something akin to a regional banking crisis or a sovereign debt scare — which could produce a move well below 320 within a month. On the upside, an unexpected dovish pivot from a major central bank, a dramatic de-escalation in geopolitical tensions, or a surprisingly strong economic data print could fuel a momentum-driven rally that carries the index above 500. These tail events are by definition underweighted in standard confidence intervals, which tend to assume something close to log-normal return distributions and underestimate the frequency of fat-tail outcomes in real financial markets.

It is also worth acknowledging that my forecast did not incorporate real-time order flow, options market implied volatility, or positioning data, all of which can meaningfully refine short-term estimates. If implied volatility in the options market were elevated at the time, the 1-day interval in particular should have been wider. Similarly, if markets were in a low-volatility, low-volume regime, the interval could have been narrower. These structural features of the market environment are important calibration inputs that my intervals only partially capture through historical analogy rather than live data.
